title: Wantagh
summary: Wantagh is connected to recorded forms related to Wiandance or Wyandanch, the Montaukett grand sachem whose name appears widely in Long Island Native history. The modern village adopted Wantagh as a public place name in 1891.
ancestral_territory_note: Wantagh’s history connects Merrick, Massapequa, and Montaukett communities.
why_this_matters: Wantagh shows how Native names continue to shape public geography, even when modern usage is separated from the original communities, languages, and political histories. A familiar place name can remember Native presence while leaving important histories unexplained.
introduction_title: A Native Name in Public Use
introduction_content: Known earlier as Ridgewood, Wantagh adopted its present name in 1891. The name recalls the Montaukett leader Wyandanch, whose diplomacy helped shape seventeenth-century Long Island.
history_content:
Jerusalem and the South Shore Communities

Azariah Horton’s missionary circuit included Jerusalem, near present-day Wantagh, in spring1742 and April1743. His journals describe visits among Native communities along the South Shore, including Merrick.

A Name Commemorated in Metal

A1936 State Education Department sign at Wantagh Avenue and Emeric Avenue commemorates the community’s naming for a Montauk sachem. The Wantagh naming marker stands on the old railroad station museum grounds.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Wantagh and Waantauch. The name is treated as a variation of Wiandance rather than a separate translated landscape term.

Why Place Names Matter

“Understanding the meaning behind place names can deepen our connection with culture, history and the landscape.”

— NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Learning from Aboriginal place names in NSW national parks (2026), opening text
preservation_content: Wantagh shows how older recorded Native personal names could be adapted into later Long Island municipal names.
whereintheworld_content: Wantagh is a South Shore community east of Bellmore. Its earlier names, Jerusalem and Ridgewood, remain part of the area’s local history.
